item.title: Alcaraz storms past world number one Zverev to win maiden ATP Finals title
item.description:

Why it is here: original reporting, clear and engaging

Alcaraz storms past world number one Zverev to win maiden ATP Finals title

Alcaraz joins an exclusive list, becoming one of only four men to have won all four majors and the ATP Finals.

Seven-time Grand Slam champion Carlos Alcaraz powered past world number one Alexander Zverev 6-2, 7-6 (9-7) on Sunday to win his maiden ATP Finals title.

The Spaniard, who returned at the US Open after a four-month break due to a wrist injury, saved three set points in the tiebreak before completing his 14th consecutive victory and ending the year with a third straight title, having also triumphed in Vienna and Paris.

The 23-year-old, who is the youngest man to have completed the career Grand Slam, secured the biggest tour title that had eluded him after finishing runner-up at the ATP Finals last year.

Since losing in the quarterfinals of the 2026 US Open, he has won four titles with a 22-1 record.

“For me, it’s been an amazing week,” Alcaraz said. “I couldn’t have ended the week in a better way. I’m just really proud and really happy with everything I have done this week.

“I’ve been through really difficult moments within myself, with my team, and we went through everything playing great tennis. This trophy is something I have been chasing for a really long time.

“It means the world to me.”

For Zverev, the defeat brought an end to his most successful season, in which he won his first two Grand Slam titles and rose to the top of the world rankings.

Alcaraz initially faced little resistance from a sluggish Zverev, who had not dropped a set en route to the final. The German struggled with his usually booming serve and made 19 unforced errors in the first set.

What had been billed as a blockbuster turned out to be a one-man show after Alcaraz bagged an early break to take control of the first set.

Zverev, a two-time ATP Finals champion, had saved all six break points he had faced during the group stage, but on Sunday he was struggling to keep pace with Alcaraz from the start.

The Spaniard earned five break points during the German’s first two service games, converting one of them. By the end of the fifth game, Zverev had racked up 15 unforced errors.

While the Spaniard buzzed around the court with his trademark intensity, chasing down every ball and nodding along to the music in the arena during the changeovers, Zverev looked sluggish and slow.

He earned one break back to cut Alcaraz’s lead to 4-2, but three points later his frustration boiled over when he argued with the umpire over a time violation warning.

The second set looked to be following a similar pattern, with Alcaraz keeping the level high and earning another early break.

But Zverev won three games on the trot to lead 5-4 and eventually forced a tiebreak. He could not convert any of his three consecutive set points, however, before Alcaraz clinched the win.

Alongside Roger Federer, Andre Agassi and Novak Djokovic, Alcaraz now forms part of an exclusive list of men to have won all four majors and the ATP Finals.

Source: Al Jazeera | Published: 2026-11-23 06:15 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Is rule-breaking contagious? The bad apple effect explained
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original research, clear explanation

Rule-breaking is contagious – and good examples barely help

Seeing someone break a rule makes people more likely to break it too, a new study finds, especially when the rule-breaker is on their side politically. Watching others behave well barely made a difference.

Most people stop at a red light, even when the road is empty. But what happens when the person next to them walks straight across?

A new study suggests they become more likely to follow. In an online experiment led by researchers at the University of Amsterdam, people who saw someone from their own political camp break a rule outright were nearly twice as likely to do the same. Seeing someone follow the rule barely made a difference.

A small number did more than copy. They broke the rule by more than the person they had watched. According to Lucas Molleman, an assistant professor of developmental psychology at the University of Amsterdam who led the research, a few bad actors like these can "basically take off the guardrails of the group."

How was the study done, and what are its limits?

The researchers wanted to know how seeing other people's choices affects whether someone sticks to a rule. They recruited 750 adults in the United States, roughly half Democrats and half Republicans, a week before the 2024 presidential election.

Participants watched an animated shooting star cross a row of 100 squares and were told to click the square where it shone brightest, which was always near the middle. Squares further to the right paid more money, so there was a reason to cheat.

Each person chose first on their own. They were then shown what a previous participant had done, whether that person had followed the rule, bent it or broken it outright, and which party they supported. Then they could change their answer. The task was repeated six times.

The experiment had no real-world stakes, and nobody was punished for cheating. Other researchers say that matters. "That's not how the world works," Eugen Dimant, a behavioral economist at the University of Pennsylvania who was not involved in the study, told Science News. Punishment and social pressure, he argues, also shape whether rule-breaking spreads.

Is rule-breaking contagious?

Rule-breaking spread in the experiment. When people chose on their own, they picked the square furthest to the right, the most lucrative and most blatant violation, about 23% of the time. After seeing someone from their own party make that choice, they did so almost 40% of the time.

Small violations had only a small effect. Blatant ones had a much larger one.

Most people matched what they had seen or stayed below it. But just over 4% went further, breaking the rule by more than the person they had watched.

Do good role models make people follow rules?

Good examples had little effect. Seeing a previous participant stick to the rule rarely changed what others did, even when that person was from their own party.

People also differed. Some followed the rule every time and others broke it every time, whatever they saw. The rest shifted depending on what others had done.

Are people more likely to break rules when their own side does?

People were more likely to copy rule-breaking when it came from their own side. The effects were stronger when the person being watched shared the participant's political leanings.

Not everyone reads that as contagion. Stephen Reicher, a social psychologist at the University of St Andrews in Scotland who was not involved in the study, told The Guardian that if influence depends on who the other person is, it does not spread the way a disease does. He pointed out that people who see a riot often turn up afterwards to help clean up.

Can a few bad apples spoil the whole group?

To see how individual choices might add up, the researchers ran computer simulations. They created a digital version of each participant and placed them in groups of 100.

In some scenarios, the handful of people prone to escalating pushed the whole group towards heavy rule-breaking. But when the simulated groups contained the same share of committed rule followers as the real experiment, rule-breaking leveled off at a moderate level.

What does this mean in real life?

Molleman calls the work fundamental science and says the real world is far more complex. He sees possible links to situations such as drivers speeding together, or protests that turn violent.

He also says it challenges how people see themselves. In individualist cultures such as the Netherlands and the UK, he said that people tend to believe they make their own decisions. But "in many, many cases we are very much influenced by what others are doing."

This article is an excerpt from our podcast Science Unscripted.

Source: DW Top Stories | Published: 2026-11-23 06:33 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: As Syria-EU talks progress, diplomats fear focus will be on repatriation
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear and engaging

As Syria-EU talks progress, diplomats fear focus will be on repatriation

Syria and the EU are in talks on trade and political ties, but migration will likely be the key issue of discussion.

Officials from Syria and the European Union are working on a deal to normalise relations after a 15-year suspension. But current and former European diplomats told Al Jazeera they fear that growing right-wing sentiments in Europe could see efforts to repatriate Syrians and immigration prioritised over other key issues, such as human rights.

Syrian and EU officials hope that a deal with the new government will lead to stronger trade and political relations, after a suspension following former President Bashar al-Assad’s brutal crackdown on protesters in 2011.

With al-Assad’s regime overthrown and a government led by President Ahmed al-Sharaa seeking closer relations with Europe, there is an opportunity for diplomatic and trade relations to resume.

“The aim is to give Europe and Syria a framework for trade, political dialogue and closer cooperation as soon as possible,” Kaja Kallas, vice president of the European Commission, said in a statement on November 16. “Syria needs investment and a successful transition.”

Analysts and diplomats told Al Jazeera that Syria’s priority in the talks was the removal of lingering EU sanctions. Brussels is largely focused on the repatriation of Syrians, with over a million fleeing to Europe during the Syrian war between 2011 and 2024. But, they added, these affairs must be managed carefully to avoid piling pressure on Syria as it continues to rebuild after war and decades of dictatorship.

“The migration issue is a big issue in Europe today,” Iyad Jaber, the Damascus-based Head of Middle East at Timios & Co and a former French diplomat of Syrian origin, told Al Jazeera. “Especially with right-wing and far-right wing [parties] taking more political space, it is moving political speech on migration.”

Deepening agreement

The first cooperation agreement between Europe and Syria was signed in 1978 by the EU’s predecessor, the European Economic Community (EEC), when Hafez al-Assad was Syria’s president. The agreement was focused on the economic and social development of Syria and a deepening of ties between the two parties.

In 2008, the EU-Syria Association Agreement was proposed but never signed by either side, largely due to concerns over the Assad government’s record on human rights. In 2011, when the government brutally repressed a popular uprising, the EU suspended ties with Syria.

During that time, the EU moved its diplomatic mission to Beirut and imposed sanctions on the Assad regime, freezing its assets and imposing travel bans on key officials.

Since the overthrow of the Assad regime, the EU has aimed to revive relations with the country. It lifted all economic sanctions on Syria last year, though some dual-use export controls and state institutions remain sanctioned.

In January, Brussels announced a two-year funding package of 620m euros ($680m) for Syria and in May the EU held its first high-level political dialogue with Syria, which aimed to revive bilateral relations.

The EU’s diplomatic service prepared a discussion paper outlining the normalisation efforts. Al Jazeera reached out to the paper’s author, but she was unavailable for comment.

Kallas said diplomats are now working through technical and legal details to finalise the agreement, which would create frameworks for free trade, political dialogue and broader cooperation between Brussels and Damascus.

Many European nations have been exploring reopening embassies or missions in Syria, diplomats told Al Jazeera, while Syrian and EU officials continue talks on normalisation and sanctions removal.

Syria’s European Affairs Directorate at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Sally Shobat, met the Head of the Middle East and North Africa Division at the European External Action Service, Jonas Jonsson, on Saturday, after earlier holding bilateral meetings with French, Cypriot and Belgian diplomatic officials.

Priorities

Since the fall of the Assad government, Syria’s new government has worked to revive suspended relations and remove sanctions imposed on its predecessor. Many of the penalties have now been removed and relations with many countries, notably members of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) and the United States, have also improved.

EU-Syrian relations may be moving in a positive direction, but experts said there are still many legal and technical obstacles to full normalisation.

“Every country has their own foreign policy,” Zakaria Al-Shmaly, a nonresident Fellow at TIMEP focusing on EU-Syria relations, told Al Jazeera.

Still, Syria has tried to prove its importance to Europe in security matters, particularly in the fight against ISIL and as an energy transit point following global disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.

“Europe needs Syria as much as Syria needs Europe,” Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa said in Nicosia in April, after an informal meeting between Syria and EU officials.

In April, al-Sharaa proposed the Four Seas and Nine Corridors Initiative, a proposed transatlantic framework connecting the Gulf, Caspian Sea, Mediterranean Sea and Black Sea via a Syria–Turkiye pipeline and transit corridor. The proposal bypasses the Strait of Hormuz for a land pipeline through Syria, following disruptions to shipping because of the US-Israeli war on Iran which began in February.

“Every power is using Syria to undermine Iran,” Al-Shmaly said.

Another key point of discussion between the EU and Syria as normalisation talks continue will be trade. Experts said Brussels will likely try to open the Syrian market to EU products, which could benefit Syrian consumers by lowering costs on certain items. However, Syrian negotiators must also consider what kind of things Syrian companies can export to the EU.…

Source: Al Jazeera | Published: 2026-11-23 06:08 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: MPs urge Miliband to force UK overseas territories to publish public company registers
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear and engaging

Ed Miliband is being urged by MPs to use his powers to force overseas territories such as the British Virgin Islands to publish public company ownership registers – almost a decade after parliament voted for transparency.

Ahead of a meeting between the foreign secretary and overseas territories this week, a cross-party group of MPs from Labour, the Tories, Lib Dems and Greens wrote to Miliband calling on him to mandate public registers of beneficial ownership of companies.

The group, coordinated by the all-party group on anti-corruption (APPG), said an improvement in corporate transparency in the overseas territories was essential after “years of broken promises and missed deadlines from certain jurisdictions, and despite repeated commitments to ending secrecy”.

They said some territories such as Gibraltar, Montserrat and St Helena had successfully opened corporate registers to the public.

But they called out the British Virgin Islands, saying it “in particular continues to let the British family down”. They said the Cayman Islands has raised its search fees to “prohibitive levels”, and Turks and Caicos have introduced huge fines for disclosing information from the register which they said was “undermining the entire purpose of open registers”.

They said that persistent engagement in good faith from the UK government has yielded few results, in the face of “outright disregard for the will of parliament”.

The BVI has a register launched this year which allows people to apply for access to ownership information if they have a “legitimate interest” such as investigating money laundering. A BVI Government spokesperson said: “We are proud of the BVI’s Legitimate Interest Access register introduced earlier this year, which allows for prompt, proportionate access, in line with international standards.

“We continue to work closely with the UK Government, delivering a major governance and regulatory reform programme to support global efforts combatting illicit finance, enforcing sanctions and recovering criminal assets - with significant progress recently recognised by the Financial Action Task Force.”

However, ahead of the meeting, the MPs including former Conservative Foreign Office minister Andrew Mitchell and Labour anti-corruption expert Phil Brickell are asking Miliband to lay an order in council mandating fully public registers of beneficial ownership in jurisdictions that continue to fail to meet their obligations.

They said it was important for UK national security “because continued secrecy undermines our ability to enforce sanctions and leaves us open to hostile state actors and criminal networks”. Second, they said developing countries continue to be destabilised and looted by kleptocrats using Britain’s own offshore financial centres to clean and stash their ill-gotten gains.

Parliament voted for open registers in 2018 and the UK government had expected public access registers to be in place in all overseas territories and crown dependencies by 2023. However, this deadline was not met.

While an order in council to mandate open registers was drafted in 2020, the government said that because there were “firm commitments” from the overseas territories to introduce public registers, the order would not be used. It said it would keep this decision under review.

Brickell, Labour chair of the APPG, said “it should never have come to this but every year of deliberate delay is another year in which kleptocrats, tax dodgers and money launderers can hide behind a British flag”.

“That is a stain on the reputation of our global family. This joint ministerial council must be the moment we finally draw a line under it.”

Mitchell, a Conservative vice-chair of the APPG and former development secretary, said: “When parliament voted for public registers in 2018, it was not making a polite request. It was the clear, cross-party will of the House of Commons, and it should have been respected.

“Instead, money stolen from some of the poorest people on earth is still being hidden behind anonymous companies in British jurisdictions. That money should be building hospitals and schools. It is paying for yachts and mansions instead, and the price is measured in lives. The British family has been patient for long enough. The foreign secretary has the power to act, and I urge him to use it.”

A Foreign Office spokesperson said: “Security is the first duty of any government. Hostile states and malign actors can exploit opaque corporate structures like those in the British Virgin Islands to hide their assets and support activity that threatens our national security.

“Ministers are actively considering how best to ensure that, where the risks are greatest, law enforcement agencies have the information they need to progress critical investigations. We will continue ongoing engagement with Overseas Territories on these issues.”

Source: The Guardian World | Published: 2026-11-23 06:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/23/mps-urge-miliband-force-uk-overseas-territories-publish-public-company-registers

item.title: How Asian countries are looking to prop up markets as AI downturn sinks stocks
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear and engaging

Market regulators in South Korea, China and Taiwan have introduced new measures aimed at supporting markets, as a tech-fueled sell-off in the region spills into another week.

On Sunday, South Korea's finance ministry said it would prepare its securities-market stabilization fund for immediate activation. The fund, reportedly established in 2020 during the Covid-19 pandemic by financial firms and other institutions seeks to support markets during sharp downturns and is valued at 10.76 trillion won (nearly $8 billion).

The government also plans to relax listed companies' daily share-buyback order limits for three months, starting Nov. 24 and start a "special intensive monitoring period" to prevent illegal short-selling. Regulators will also track margin lending and forced liquidations.

South Korean stocks have seen wild swings over 2026 as investors piled into, then fled from its two tech heavyweights, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, both critical companies in the AI supply chain. The benchmark Kospi index is deep in bear territory, down more than 46% from its June high.

The ministry said that it "assessed that volatility in domestic and international stock markets has significantly increased recently due to internal and external uncertainties surrounding the global AI and semiconductor industries, as well as U.S. interest rate hikes," according to a Google translation of the release in Korean.

However, Seoul also said that the mid-to-long-term growth expectations for the AI industry remain intact, and that "excessive anxiety is not a concern."

Taiwan, which is also exposed to the AI industry through Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company and other tech firms, has also moved to rein in market volatility.

Taiwan's Financial Supervisory Commission announced Friday that short selling below the closing price was "completely prohibited," while making it an exception if used for hedging purposes by securities and futures firms.

"Investors must not sell listed (OTC) stocks or Taiwan Depositary Receipts at a price lower than the closing price of the previous trading day," the FSC said, according to a Google translation of the statement in Chinese.

Margin requirements for short selling will also be increased, and applications from securities firms to issue warrants for listing will be suspended, as the regulator aims to curb speculative activity.

In a similar move to Seoul, Taipei encouraged firms to buy back stocks, adding that the purchases will be included in the companies' environmental, social and governance scores if completed between the fourth quarter of 2026 and the first quarter of 2027.

The island's stock market is heavily dominated by its tech industry, most notably, chip manufacturing giant TSMC. The stock fell 15% last week, while the index dropped 17.5%.

While South Korea and Taiwan are looking to curb speculative trading to arrest the slide in their markets, Beijing is looking to encourage more leverage-based buying.

The Shanghai Stock Exchange said on Sunday that exchanges in Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing will cut the minimum margin ratio for margin-financed stock purchases to 80% from 100%, starting Nov. 30. That means investors will be able to borrow more for their stock market bets.

The Shanghai and Shenzhen exchanges also announced fee cuts, while Shenzhen proposed a market-making mechanism for its ChiNext board. The steps will help inject more liquidity into the market that has also born the brunt of the souring in tech and AI trade, with the benchmark CSI 300 index closing lower for 14 of the past 15 weeks.

Seoul's markets led losses in the region, with the Kospi down over 3.26%. Smaller losses were seen in mainland China's CSI 300, which declined 0.71%. The Taiwan Weighted Index, however, reversed earlier losses to gain over 2% on Monday.

item.title: New Zealand’s Mitchell, Phillips frustrate India as first Test ends in draw
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear and engaging

New Zealand’s Mitchell, Phillips frustrate India as first Test ends in draw

New Zealand rescued a draw on the final day, surviving 120 overs in a fighting display to finish on 239-5 at the close.

New Zealand fought a rearguard action to deny India as the first Test in Wellington ended in a draw on Monday, with the tourists five wickets short of converting their mammoth first-innings lead into victory.

India entered the final day needing eight dismissals to take a 1-0 lead in the series and boost their World Test Championship (WTC) hopes, but New Zealand were down to their last two specialist batters at tea.

New Zealand were 239-5 in their second innings, still trailing India’s first-innings 720-9 declared by 113 runs, when the captains shook hands to end the contest.

Daryl Mitchell, who made 49 not out, and first-innings centurion Glenn Phillips (26) put on 63 for the sixth wicket on a Basin Reserve track that had been all but lifeless since the opening session and a bit of the match.

“I think we knew it was going to be a challenge to get 10 wickets on that wicket,” said India captain Shubman Gill.

“I didn’t really think having five or 10 extra overs would have helped that much. We also wanted to keep our bowlers fresh with the quick turnaround.”

India will take some confidence from their batting performance as they head to Christchurch for the second Test, starting on Friday, after six players each scored a half-century or better in a single innings.

KL Rahul (136) and Rishabh Pant (128) both hit centuries in contrasting styles, while Gill fell two runs short of the milestone.

Pace spearhead Jasprit Bumrah impressed on his return to Test cricket after a year out, helping reduce New Zealand to 70-5 on the opening day, although he was used sparingly as India chased the result on Monday.

Phillips, Mitchell occupy the crease

New Zealand’s match was a tale of two sixth-wicket stands, the first of 216 runs between Henry Nicholls (175 not out) and Phillips (118) that enabled the hosts to post a respectable 368 in their first knock.

The second between Phillips and Mitchell on Monday was never going to be about the tally of runs but more about how long they occupied the crease.

“Throughout the week, we’ve had some guys put their hands up,” said New Zealand captain Tom Latham.

“Not just today but also throughout that first innings. We had our backs against the wall a little bit coming into that third innings, so to be in this position now, yeah, pretty pleased.”

Phillips and Mitchell came together in the sixth over after lunch when Tom Blundell departed for 15 off the bowling of Anshul Kamboj to leave New Zealand at 176-5.

The delivery appeared to have beaten the bat before going through to wicketkeeper Pant, but Kamboj heard something, and when India reviewed, the DRS technology revealed the faintest of nicks.

In the opening session, spinner Washington Sundar made the first breakthrough by removing Devon Conway for 65, the ball popping up off the opener’s bat and pad for Pant to collect with an athletic catch.

Rachin Ravindra, the other overnight batter, followed for 37 with a miscued shot off the bowling of seamer Prasidh Krishna that flew to Rahul in the slips.

India will rue a few missed chances to make further inroads into the New Zealand batting order, most notably a potential run-out that would have sent Mitchell back early in his innings.

The draw means New Zealand drop out of the top two in the 2025-27 WTC standings, with Australia moving up to join leaders and reigning champions South Africa. India remain fourth.

item.title: At least 24 killed and dozens missing in confectionery factory fire in Indonesia
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear and engaging

Indonesia has confirmed the deaths of 24 people in a fire that tore through a factory, as rescuers braved unstable structures in the burned wreckage to search for about 30 people still missing.

Authorities were still investigating the cause of the fire, which broke out on Saturday in the PT Fonusa Agung Mulia confectionery factory in Cikande in Banten province, about 50km west of Jakarta.

Said Iqbal, a presidential adviser on labour issues, told reporters 24 people had died. He said the implementation of safety protocols was being assessed and that he would summon the factory’s chief executive.

Preliminary reports indicated the fire might have been caused by an air-conditioner short circuit, Said added. The factory is owned by United Family Food, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The condition of the victims made visual identification impossible, prompting authorities to urge family members to provide DNA samples and other information that could be used to identify their loved ones, said Wahyu Hidayati Dwi Palupi, who heads the national police’s victim identification division.

She said body bags containing the remains of the victims were transferred to a hospital for identification.

The blaze had largely been contained on Sunday but firefighters were carrying out intensive cooling operations on Monday before they could access all parts of the factory, said Tubagus Mahfud, operations chief of the Serang fire department.

“We are conducting sweeps in the areas that have already been brought under control,” Mahfud said. “Parts of the structure had collapsed, while poor lighting conditions required firefighters to proceed cautiously.”

He also said the factory’s production materials could cause the fire to reignite, making it critical to complete cooling operations.

Anxious relatives have waited for news outside the burnt-out factory.

The Banten province governor, Andra Soni, said an estimated 60 people were inside the factory when it caught fire.

The firm employs about 5,000 people and is a major supplier of consumer goods to the domestic market. Its products include Milkita, a popular confectionery brand, and Lemonilo, an instant noodle variety, according to its website.

The company’s chief executive, Steven Wijaya, said the factory regularly conducted emergency and evacuation drills in conjunction with local firefighters. He said the facility had adequate evacuation routes and fire protection systems that complied with applicable safety standards and were functioning at the time of the fire.

Indonesia has experienced a series of deadly industrial fires in recent years, raising concerns about workplace safety standards and emergency preparedness at manufacturing facilities.

In December last year, a blaze that was likely caused by a drone battery explosion tore through a seven-storey building in Jakarta and killed at least 22 people, police said.

In 2023, at least 13 people were killed in the country’s east after an explosion at a nickel-processing plant.
